id: Relaxing or Voluntarily Having Dumb, Unpleasant Experiences

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Some people like to relax and kick back with their friends just talking and having a drink which is obviously highly pleasurable. Some people like to be entertained by music or a movie; some people like to make some jokes with people they like, maybe at a bar or at someone’s house. Some people like to lay around with another person, just touching, or to prepare food, alone or with others while listening to music that they feel a particular affinity for. But sometimes people like to thrust themselves into the howling wind and snow, arms tied behind their backs. I prefer to open my mouth wide open knowing what will happen if I’m just holding my mouth open, ready to respond or yell or whatever seems appropriate. You know, I keep my mouth at the ready to make a lot of noise. And sometimes it becomes filled with hard packed snow or with sand, sand being more of a problem, since, you know, it won’t melt.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Some people find pleasure in relaxing with friends, talking, drinking, and enjoying social connection.
- Others prefer entertainment such as music, movies, jokes, or spending time with people they like.
- Some people enjoy quieter sensory activities like lying with another person, touching, or preparing food while listening to meaningful music.
- The speaker contrasts these comforts with a preference for extreme experiences, such as facing harsh wind and snow with arms tied behind their back.
- The speaker describes keeping their mouth open and ready to make noise, even though it may become filled with snow or sand.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores contrasting forms of pleasure and experience, moving from ordinary social relaxation to a vivid first-person description of deliberately enduring harsh wind, snow, and sand. It suggests that some people seek intensity or discomfort rather than comfort, highlighting the strange, personal, and sometimes impractical ways humans pursue sensation.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Some, But, You

outputs.L1:
Some people enjoy relaxing and unwinding with friends—simply talking and sharing a drink—which is, of course, highly pleasurable. Others prefer to be entertained by music or a film; some like to joke with people they care about, perhaps at a bar or in someone’s home. Some enjoy lying around with another person, simply touching, or preparing food, alone or with others, while listening to music for which they feel a particular affinity.

But sometimes, people like to thrust themselves into the howling wind and snow, their arms tied behind their backs. I prefer to open my mouth wide, fully aware of what may happen if I simply hold it open—ready to respond, or yell, or do whatever seems appropriate. I keep my mouth at the ready, prepared to make a great deal of noise. And sometimes it becomes filled with hard-packed snow, or with sand—sand being more of a problem, since, of course, it will not melt.
outputs.L2:
Many people enjoy unwinding with friends by simply chatting over a drink, which is naturally very enjoyable. Others prefer amusement in the form of music or a film. Some like joking around with people they are fond of, perhaps in a bar or at someone’s home. Others enjoy lying beside another person and touching, or cooking either by themselves or with company while playing music they feel especially connected to.

At other times, however, people choose to throw themselves into screaming wind and snow with their arms bound behind them. As for me, I tend to keep my mouth stretched open, fully aware of what may happen when I do that, prepared to answer, shout, or make whatever sound feels suitable. In other words, I keep my mouth ready to produce a great deal of noise. Occasionally it ends up packed with dense snow, or with sand—which is worse, because, of course, sand does not melt.
outputs.L3:
Many people find pleasure in simple moments of relaxation and companionship. For some, happiness comes from sitting with friends, talking freely, sharing drinks, and enjoying the warmth of social connection. These experiences offer comfort because they create a sense of belonging and ease.

Other people prefer different forms of entertainment. They may enjoy listening to music, watching movies, laughing at jokes, or spending time with people whose company they genuinely like. For them, pleasure is found in amusement, shared laughter, and the familiar enjoyment of being around others.

There are also those who are drawn to quieter, more sensory experiences. They may find comfort in lying beside another person, feeling physical closeness, touching, or preparing food while meaningful music plays in the background. These activities are gentle and intimate, creating a peaceful atmosphere that appeals to the senses and emotions.

The speaker, however, contrasts these common forms of comfort with a very different preference. Instead of seeking relaxation, entertainment, or tenderness, the speaker is drawn to extreme and uncomfortable experiences. They describe a desire to face harsh wind and snow with their arms tied behind their back, suggesting a preference for intensity, exposure, and challenge rather than ease.

The speaker also describes keeping their mouth open, ready to make noise, even if it becomes filled with snow or sand. This image emphasizes endurance and defiance. Rather than avoiding discomfort, the speaker seems prepared to confront it directly, accepting even harsh physical conditions as part of the experience.
outputs.L4:
Pleasure does not always take the same form. For many people, it is easy to recognize in familiar settings: a warm room, good food, easy conversation, music in the background, and the company of friends. This kind of enjoyment is social, comfortable, and ordinary. It asks little of the body beyond relaxation. It depends on softness, warmth, and a sense of being protected from difficulty. In such moments, pleasure seems almost the same as ease.

Yet there is another kind of experience that is harder to explain. Some people are not satisfied by comfort alone. They seek out intensity, even when that intensity appears unpleasant or irrational to others. Instead of avoiding cold, wind, snow, or rough weather, they deliberately place themselves in it. They may walk into a storm, feel sand striking their skin, or stand against a bitter wind as if testing the limits of their own endurance. What would seem miserable to one person may become, for another, a source of excitement, clarity, or even joy.

In a vivid first-person account of such an experience, the speaker describes exposing the body to harsh natural forces. The wind is not gentle; it cuts and presses. Snow and sand do not merely surround the person but seem to attack, scraping the face and making movement difficult. The experience is uncomfortable, even painful, yet it is not presented simply as suffering. The speaker chooses it. The discomfort becomes meaningful because it is deliberate. It sharpens awareness. Every sensation becomes immediate: the sting of cold, the resistance of the air, the roughness of particles against the skin, the effort required to keep moving.

This contrast reveals something strange about human desire. People do not always pursue what is easiest or most pleasant in the ordinary sense. Sometimes they seek experiences that interrupt comfort and force them to feel intensely alive. Discomfort can become attractive when it offers a break from routine or a sense of contact with something powerful and real. The body, usually protected and sheltered, is suddenly made aware of itself. The person is no longer merely resting or passing time but struggling, sensing, and enduring.

Such behavior can seem impractical. There is no obvious reward in standing in freezing wind or letting sand sting one’s face. It does not produce money, status, or convenience. From the outside, it may even look foolish. But human beings often pursue sensation for reasons that cannot be reduced to usefulness. They climb mountains, swim in cold water, run long distances, enter deserts, or expose themselves to storms because these experiences offer something beyond comfort. They provide intensity, self-knowledge, and the pleasure of testing one’s own limits.

The text therefore suggests that pleasure is deeply personal and sometimes paradoxical. One person’s misery may be another person’s delight. The comfort of a relaxed social gathering and the harsh thrill of facing wind, snow, and sand may seem opposite, but both belong to the wide range of human experience. Together, they show that people are not driven only by the desire to feel good in a simple sense. They also seek moments that are strange, difficult, and vivid—moments that make them feel the full force of being alive.
outputs.L5: Some days feel simple, while others bring unexpected challenges. But every moment offers a chance to learn, grow, and see things from a new perspective. You may not always have control over what happens, but you can choose how to respond. With patience, confidence, and a positive mindset, even small steps can lead to meaningful progress.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, conversational monologue about different ways people seek pleasure, ending with a bizarre preference involving wind, snow, and sand filling the speaker’s mouth.
counterfactuals.output:
People are funny about pleasure, aren’t they?

Some people want it neat, folded into a linen napkin beside a tiny spoon. They want a restaurant where the lights are low enough to forgive everybody, where the soup arrives with a little green island floating in it, and someone says, “This was reduced for sixteen hours,” as if time itself has been boiled down for their benefit.

Other people want speed. They want the motorcycle, the elevator drop, the moment the plane lifts and your stomach stays behind like an unpaid bill. They want to feel their skeleton ring like a tuning fork. They want the world to shout their name incorrectly.

Some people seek pleasure in being admired. They stand under chandeliers of attention and turn slowly, like rotisserie saints. Compliments land on them like warm coins. They save them in secret jars. Later, alone, they shake the jars and listen.

Others want quiet. A chair. A cat. Rain practicing scales on the roof. The immense luxury of not being asked anything. They want to dissolve into a blanket and become a rumor the room tells itself.

There are people who find pleasure in buying shoes, in sharpening knives, in alphabetizing spices, in saying no, in being forgiven, in not forgiving, in lying facedown on clean sheets while a fan turns overhead like a lazy god deciding whether to invent weather.

And love, of course. People chase that with nets, with poems, with perfume, with entire personalities constructed overnight from panic and hope. They want another person to look at them and say, “Yes, you. Somehow, you.” Which is very sweet, and also a little like asking a mirror to become a homeland.

Me? I’ve tried the usual things. Chocolate, applause, hot baths, revenge fantasies in which everyone is impressed by how calmly I leave. They’re fine. Perfectly fine.

But if I’m honest, what I really prefer is standing in a field during impossible weather, letting the wind shove snow and sand into my face until my mouth fills with winter and desert at the same time, and I can’t speak, and I can’t explain myself, and the whole world tastes like a broken hourglass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange first-person paragraph that starts by listing ordinary relaxing activities with friends, then pivots into an absurd description of enjoying harsh weather with arms tied behind the back.
counterfactuals.output: I like spending time with my friends in the usual soft ways: sipping coffee on quiet afternoons, watching old movies under blankets, wandering through bookstores, sharing lazy dinners, laughing over board games, and taking slow walks when the sun is kind. But sometimes, for reasons I cannot explain, my idea of peace becomes standing in a sideways storm with my arms tied behind my back, grinning into the rain as hail taps out a tiny percussion solo on my forehead, while the wind shouts ancient nonsense into my ears and I nod along like it is telling me the funniest secret in the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rambling, slightly comic prose piece in which the narrator compares normal social pleasures like drinks, music, movies, jokes, touch, and cooking to their own peculiar habit of standing in storms with their mouth open.
counterfactuals.output:
People are forever recommending pleasures to me, as though I have arrived on earth insufficiently equipped and must be fitted at once with the proper handles. They say, “Come for drinks,” and I do go, sometimes, because I am not a monster, only damp. I stand in someone’s kitchen holding a glass of wine by the stem, which makes me feel briefly civilized, like a heron at a diplomatic reception. Everyone laughs and leans against counters. Someone has brought olives. Someone else has opinions about vermouth. The ice makes that little expensive music in the bucket. It is all very nice, and I can see why civilization has arranged itself around fermented liquids in transparent containers.

But there is a moment, usually after the second person has said “oaky,” when I think: yes, yes, but have you ever stood in a thunderstorm with your mouth open?

I do not mean this as a metaphor, though people always assume I do, because it is apparently illegal now to enjoy anything literally. I mean actually: shoes sinking slightly into the lawn, hair pasted to the skull, shirt clinging to one’s sides with the proprietary attitude of a relative at a funeral, face tilted upward, mouth wide as a baby bird or a drainpipe, receiving the sky. Rainwater has a taste, you know. Not a good taste, exactly. I am not recommending it as a beverage. It tastes of altitude, dust, tin roofs, leaves, and the faint moral disapproval of clouds. It is wonderfully under-seasoned.

Music is another one. People love music, and I do understand. A violin can behave in such a way that one suspects it has seen the inside of a human soul and found the lighting poor. Drums can persuade even the shyest person that hips were invented for reasons other than trouser suspension. At weddings, music performs its usual miracle: it convinces uncles to clap on beats no scientist has yet discovered. I have been moved by music. I have stood in dark rooms with a hundred strangers while a singer held a note like a candle in the wind, and I have thought, here we are, all of us, dignified ruins.

Still, thunder has a bass section that no orchestra has managed. It enters not through the ear but through the sternum, the floorboards, the fillings of one’s teeth. It rolls over the houses as if God, or someone in management, is dragging furniture across heaven. Then comes the rain, applauding every surface at once. Leaves. Gutters. Pavement. My forehead. The whole world becomes percussion, and I stand there with my mouth open, contributing nothing but enthusiasm.

Movies are pleasant too. I like the ceremony of them: the velvet darkness, the shared popcorn, the glowing faces all pointed toward the same enormous lie. In films, people have cheekbones in weather. They run through airports and always arrive at the gate just as some emotional truth is being announced over the public address system. They kiss in the rain, of course, because cinema understands that water falling from the sky improves nearly every human activity except accounting.

But in a real storm, there is no plot, which I find restful. No one is revealed to be the rightful heir to a bakery. No detective discovers that the murderer was grief all along. The storm does not care whether I had a difficult childhood or failed to answer an email. It simply arrives, enormous and badly organized, and falls on everything equally: the virtuous, the fraudulent, the hydrangeas, the grill cover, me. Especially me, if I have planned correctly.

Jokes are another great pleasure, and I admire anyone who can tell one properly. A good joke is a machine built to detonate dignity. It begins politely, sets out a little carpet of expectation, invites you to walk across, and then drops you through a trapdoor into delight. I have laughed so hard at jokes that I made the wheezing sound of an accordion being stepped on by a man late for a train. I do not undervalue jokes.

Yet there is comedy in storms that no human comic can equal. Consider me, for example: an adult person, taxpayer, occasional wearer of matching socks, standing alone in the yard with my jaw unhinged like a stunned cod. The neighbors pretend not to see. Their curtains develop opinions. Dogs bark with that tone that means, “This is outside the terms of our agreement.” Once, a passing jogger slowed down—not stopped, which would have been humane, but slowed, preserving the option of escape—and asked, “Are you okay?” I gave him a thumbs-up, though with my mouth open and rain pouring in, it may have looked less like reassurance than a medical episode.

Touch, of course, is supposed to be one of the great consolations. A hand on the shoulder. A kiss on the back of the neck. A friend’s arm linked through yours while crossing a street neither of you feared until that moment. Touch says: here you are, and here is someone else, and the boundary between you is not a prison wall but a garden fence with a loose gate. I am fond of touch, in theory and often in practice, provided everyone has washed and no one is surprising me from behind while I am carrying soup.

But rain is touch multiplied beyond propriety. It is a thousand cold fingers, none of them asking how work is going. It does not stroke; it stipples. It taps the eyelids, needles the scalp, trickles absurdly down the spine with the confidence of someone who has a key. It gets under collars and into cuffs and behind ears. It is intimate without being romantic, which is a category society has not sufficiently explored. A storm embraces you the way an overexcited aunt embraces you at a station: too hard, too wet, smelling faintly of travel.

Cooking is perhaps the most respectable pleasure of all, because it produces evidence. You chop, sauté, reduce, plate. There is steam and garlic and the rich authority of butter. People gather. They say, “What smells so good?” and you, the temporary household deity, pretend modesty while knowing perfectly well it is the onions. I admire cooking deeply. It turns ingredients into forgiveness. It makes a room feel inhabited by benevolent ancestors, even if you learned the recipe from a video called “One-Pan Weeknight Thing.”

But cooking requires intention. Storm-mouth-standing requires only weather and a willingness to disappoint one’s species. There is no recipe. You cannot overdo it, except by drowning, which is generally frowned upon. You cannot substitute hail for rain unless you are looking for a dental adventure. You simply wait for the sky to darken, for the air to go greenish and theatrical, for the trees to show the pale undersides of their leaves like startled palms. Then you step outside.

And oh, that first drop. It lands on the tongue with the solemnity of a telegram. Then another. Then the whole vast message arrives, illegible and urgent. I stand there receiving it, swallowing bits of cloud, grinning like a fool at the gutters overflowing. Somewhere indoors, reasonable people are pouring drinks, putting on records, choosing films, kissing, laughing, stirring sauces, living the beautiful catalog of ordinary pleasures. I salute them. I wish them well. I may even join them later, once I have toweled off and been made to stand on newspaper.

But for now I am occupied. The storm has opened its mouth too, and between us there is a conversation without words, without manners, and without even the smallest olive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In a casual “you know” style, write about how people relax in different ways, but make the narrator prefer an uncomfortable outdoor scenario involving howling wind, hard-packed snow, and sand.
counterfactuals.output:
People relax in all kinds of ways, you know?

Some people want a soft couch, a warm blanket, maybe a show they’ve already seen twelve times so they don’t have to think too hard. Some people light candles and take a bath like they’re in a shampoo commercial. Other people go to cafes, order something with foam on it, and sit there pretending they’re writing a novel when really they’re just scrolling.

And that’s all fine. Totally normal.

But me? I don’t know, I relax best when things are a little miserable.

Like, give me a wide-open stretch of nowhere with the wind howling so hard it feels personal. Give me hard-packed snow under my boots, the kind that doesn’t crunch so much as scrape. Throw in sand, too, because why not make it weird? Sand blowing low across the snow, stinging your ankles, getting into every seam of your clothes even though it has absolutely no business being there.

That’s peaceful to me, somehow.

No soft music, no scented oils, no fluffy robe. Just me squinting into the wind, my face half-numb, my hands shoved into my pockets, thinking, “Yeah, okay. This is good.”

Maybe it’s because there’s nothing to do out there except stand your ground. The weather is loud enough to shut up all the little thoughts. The cold keeps you honest. The sand keeps you annoyed in a very specific, grounding way.

So while everybody else is relaxing by getting comfortable, I guess I relax by finding a place that’s openly hostile and letting it push back a little. You know, just to feel normal again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an offbeat stream-of-consciousness passage about leisure and pleasure that gradually becomes unsettling and absurd, with the speaker explaining why sand in the mouth is worse than snow.
counterfactuals.output:
Leisure begins with a chair, I think, a chair in the sun and a drink with a little paper umbrella, though the umbrella is useless because nothing in the glass is worried about rain. I am worried about rain. Not a lot. Just professionally. The clouds have been acting like managers.

Pleasure is supposed to be soft. It is towels warmed by invisible hands, the lazy arithmetic of afternoon, one plum, then no plum, then the sweet red evidence on the thumb. Pleasure is lying down in grass and letting the ants believe they have discovered a continent. I have always admired ants for their optimism. They find a knee and immediately begin mapping it, as if there will be ports, taxation, a parliament.

But then there is the beach.

Everyone says the beach is leisure, and perhaps it is, if you are the sort of person who can ignore a million pulverized bones trying to enter you. Sand is not a surface. Sand is a conspiracy of tiny insistences. It goes into shoes, ears, sandwiches, marriages. It waits in the seam of a towel like a grudge with texture. You can rinse it off, yes, but only in the way you can apologize to a ghost: ceremonially, without results.

Snow, by contrast, is at least honest. Snow enters the mouth and becomes water. It has an exit strategy. It may be cold, humiliating, even faintly theatrical, but it knows when to leave. Snow says, “Forgive me, I was only passing through.” Sand says nothing. Sand attends the meeting indefinitely. Sand in the mouth is worse than snow because snow surrenders to the body, while sand remains itself, a collection of small dry verdicts grinding between the teeth. Snow becomes memory. Sand becomes an argument you keep losing.

This is why I do not trust sandcastles. They are castles made of things that want to be in your gums.

Still, people laugh at the shore. They roast themselves pink and call it health. They close their eyes while the ocean drags its large blue tongue up the land again and again, tasting for a weakness. Children dig holes. Adults say, “Don’t dig too deep,” which is funny, because what is too deep? At a certain depth, every hole becomes biography. At a certain depth, the beach remembers what it was before towels and radio music and the man selling mango slices from a cooler that hums though it has no motor.

I once fell asleep under an umbrella and dreamed I was being seasoned.

When I woke, my tongue was full of sand. Not a lot, not a shovel, not a desert, but enough. Enough to make chewing sound like footsteps in an empty house. Enough to make me understand oysters, clocks, old kings. I spat and spat, and the beach watched me with its many bright grains, each one a little eye or tooth or idea. A gull stood nearby, wearing the expression of a lawyer who has just found a loophole in the concept of mercy.

“Snow would never do this,” I told the gull.

The gull opened its beak, and out came the noise of a chair scraping across a room upstairs.

This is when the leisure began to curdle. The sun lowered itself like an orange coin into a vending machine, but nothing came out. The sea kept advancing and retreating, advancing and retreating, practicing indecision on a planetary scale. Behind me, the boardwalk lights blinked on, one by one, like a row of people pretending not to recognize me. Somewhere a child laughed, then laughed again, exactly the same way, then again, until it was clearly not laughter but a mechanism testing its range.

I packed my towel. The towel was heavier than before.

At home, I found sand in the pockets of clothes I had not brought to the beach. Sand in the sugar bowl. Sand in the little groove around the bathtub drain. Sand under my tongue, though I had brushed my teeth until my gums sang hymns. Snow would have vanished. Snow would have melted into the plumbing and joined the general wetness of the world. But sand had ambition. Sand had tenure.

Now, when I seek pleasure, I choose safer things: lukewarm soup, documentaries about furniture, the velvet darkness inside a peach. I sit in my chair and sip my drink and watch the paper umbrella tremble though there is no wind. Sometimes, in the quiet, I hear it: the faint granular applause from the cupboard, the pantry, the walls.

Tiny hands, clapping.

Or teeth.

Or both.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
